newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan telecom giants differ in business outlook.
newsitem.headline: Japan telecom giants differ in business outlook.

text.p: Japanese telecommunications giant NTT Corp expects profits to grow next business year, buoyed by new services such as Internet access, but the outlook seems less bright for international carrier KDD.

The two telecoms leaders, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) and Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd (KDD), unveiled contrasting business forecasts on Friday for the year starting on April 1, reflecting massive changes in Japan's telecommunications market.

While NTT said it expects its parent current profit to grow by 1.4 percent, KDD expects its to fall by almost 20 percent. Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses from securities investments and other non-operating activities.
KDD also revised down its profit forecast for this business year, while NTT kept its unchanged.

NTT, which last November surprised the stock market with its bullish business forecasts, said its profit would continue to grown in the year to the end of March 1998, despite recent large rate cuts, because of strong revenues from Internet and cellular phone users.
"We will be able to maintain profit and sales increases in the next business year," NTT executive vice president Shuichi Kizuka told a news conference.
NTT forecast a 1.4 percent gain in parent current profit to 354 billion yen ($2.92 billion) next fiscal year, but some analysts think this too conservative.
"This is a very conservative forecast," said Toshiaki Iba, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson (Asia) Ltd.

"We expect NTT's current profit to easily top 400 billion yen ($3.3 billion) next business year," Iba said, citing a prospect of a more than 10 percent gain in NTT's local-call traffic next year helped by Internet users.
NTT, which is 65 percent owned by the government, monopolises Japan's local-call networks.
Kizuka said NTT should gain one million new customers for its integrated services digital network (ISDN) lines next year, pushing up ISDN revenues by 80 billion yen ($661 million).
KDD, on the other hand, which serves Japan's small international call market, has been hit hard by rate cuts it announced last autumn and tougher competition.
It said its sales and profits would fall next business year for the second consecutive year. It also revised down sales and profit estimates for the current year ending on March 31.

A spread of counterfeit telephone cards, which forced NTT to stop offering international services from public phones, also dealt a blow to KDD, KDD's managing director Kazuyuki Tsukada told a news conference.
"Revenues from international phone traffic did not grow as we had expected, although there were some bright spots, like increasing revenues from Internet connection services," he said.
KDD said its parent current profit for the next business year would fall 19 percent to 17 billion yen ($140 million), while sales would decrease 2 percent to 323 billion yen ($2.66 billion).

It revised down parent current profit estimates for the current year to 21 billion yen ($173 million) from the 24 billion yen ($198 million) it forecast last November and an actual profit of 31.25 billion yen ($258 million) in 1995/96.
NTT's parent current profit forecast of 349 billion yen ($2.88 billion) for the current fiscal year was unchanged from its November forecast.
Dresdner's Iba said KDD may also be forced to revise down its 1997/98 forecast since the government plans to deregulate the international resale of leased lines in October.
"With competition from NTT and big overseas carriers expected following the deregulation, KDD could suffer tough market conditions for a while," Iba said.
KDD said it plans a record 104 billion yen ($859 million) in capital spending for the next business year to buoy its entry into the domestic long-distance phone market. ($1=121 yen)
